# Vacuum tube (diode, triode, amplifier) (`vacuum_tube`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/electricity.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Electricity & electronics (`electricity`)
- Deps: needs electric_light, air_pump_vacuum; helped by electromagnetic_waves_radio, atomic_structure, ohms_law_circuits
- Core idea: A glowing filament in a highly evacuated glass bulb gives off electrons. A metal plate in the bulb collects them when it is positive and repels them when negative, so current passes one way only (diode, rectifier). A wire mesh or spiral between filament and plate, the grid, controls the stream: a small change of voltage on the grid, taking almost no current, causes a large change in the plate current, so the tube amplifies. With part of the output fed back to the input through a tuned circuit it oscillates and generates continuous waves. The vacuum must be far better than in early lamps, with the metal parts baked during pumping and a getter of barium or magnesium flashed inside to bind the remaining gas.
- Pitfalls:
  - A soft vacuum: leftover gas ionises, the tube behaves erratically and the filament is destroyed; De Forest's first audions suffered from this and he misunderstood how they worked
  - Forgetting that the grid must stay negative with respect to the filament, or it draws current and distorts
  - Underrating heat, power use and limited life; thousands of tubes mean daily failures, which is the main reason to look for a solid-state replacement
  - Believing that the triode was understood from the start; its use as amplifier and oscillator came only in 1912–1913
- History: americas: 1880–1883 – Edison notes current crossing the vacuum in a lamp (Edison effect); 1906 De Forest's audion, a gassy triode; 1912–1913 Arnold at AT&T and Langmuir at General Electric make high-vacuum tubes; 1912 Armstrong's regenerative circuit; europe: 1897 – J. J. Thomson identifies the electron; 1904 Fleming's diode valve (London); 1906 von Lieben's amplifying valve (Vienna); 1913 Meissner's valve oscillator
- Read:
  - Gerald F. J. Tyne, Saga of the Vacuum Tube (1977)
  - Sungook Hong, Wireless: From Marconi's Black-Box to the Audion (2001)
